idiom_name: guard object holding a lambda (Alexandrescu ScopeGuard shape), `std::experimental::scope_exit` / `boost::scope::scope_exit` / gsl::finally
implementation_notes: C++ needs no library for this pattern: any local object whose destructor invokes a stored callable is a scope guard, and destructors run on every exit path including stack unwinding, in reverse order of construction - so the guard is constructed after the resource and destroyed before it. The canonical modern form is a small non-copyable guard template holding a lambda with a release()/dismiss() step for commit; the Library Fundamentals v3 header <experimental/scope> standardizes exactly that as std::experimental::scope_exit plus scope_fail/scope_success with release(), and Boost.Scope ships the same components as boost::scope::scope_exit / make_scope_exit with set_active(false). The hand-written guard object is still justified when the toolchain predates C++17, when no Boost/TS vocabulary type should be introduced, or when the guard must also own the resource - in that case it is an ordinary RAII owner rather than a pure action guard.
pitfalls: Construction order is release order: a guard declared before the resource it protects destroys the resource first (reverse order of construction), so the guard must follow its resource in the scope.

If the exit function refers to a local that is used as a return operand, that local may already have been returned when the guard runs - cppreference documents this for std::experimental::scope_exit, and it is the same dangling-capture trap for hand-written guards.

An exit function that throws while the stack is unwinding calls std::terminate, and constructing a scope guard with dynamic storage duration is documented to behave unexpectedly - guards belong on the stack.

variants.name: Standardized/library scope guards (Library Fundamentals v3, Boost.Scope)
variants.implementation_notes: Use the library guard types instead of a local template: std::experimental::scope_exit from <experimental/scope> (already active when constructed from the exit function, release() deactivates it for commit, scope_fail and scope_success run only on the failing or the normal path) or Boost.Scope's make_scope_exit / scope_exit / scope_fail with set_active(false). Choose this variant when the toolchain provides the TS header or Boost and you want defined move semantics plus the exit classifiers for free; keep the hand-written guard for pre-C++17 toolchains or when a third-party vocabulary type must not enter the codebase.
pitfalls: <experimental/scope> is a Technical Specification header: it is not part of the published standard (the C++26 library features list does not contain scope_exit) and implementations gate it behind their own feature-test macros, so the toolchain expectation must be explicit.

The guard types are not CopyConstructible, CopyAssignable or MoveAssignable: moving one deactivates the source, so returning a guard from a factory gives the caller an inactive guard that silently does nothing.

variants.name: Boost.ScopeExit macro guards (pre-C++11 toolchains)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.ScopeExit declares the exit body inline where the resource is acquired: BOOST_SCOPE_EXIT(captures) { ... } BOOST_SCOPE_EXIT_END captures the listed variables and runs the body when the enclosing scope exits, with several scope exits in one scope executed in reverse order of declaration; BOOST_SCOPE_EXIT_TPL is the template form. There is no dismiss operation, so commit is expressed by a captured flag that the body reads. Choose it only for pre-C++11 toolchains where lambdas are unavailable - Boost.Scope or a plain guard object is clearer on any modern compiler.
pitfalls: The body is expanded at the declaration point and captures by reference: a captured variable that leaves the scope earlier than the guard is a dangling reference when the body finally runs.
Several scope exits in one scope run in reverse order of declaration, but none of them can be dismissed - commit semantics must be modelled with an explicit flag that the body reads.
